EXP-38 — Dense GRPO temporal-drift probe dataset: BIG-MATH

How fast does the on-policy GRPO learning signal drift in time — in gradient space, the boundary-activation subspace, and rollout/behaviour space — and what does that imply for the next communication-efficient pipeline-parallel GRPO method? This report covers the BIG-MATH dataset ONLY.

Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct · BIG-MATH · accel surface (response cap 16384, dynamic-bsz, TP1) · dense (comm_eff OFF) · 75 global steps = 150 optimizer ticks · n=1 trajectory · lag axis in optimizer ticks (2 ticks/global-step ⇒ k≈5 ≙ the stable 5/5 anchor, k≈20 ≙ the broken 20/20 anchor, k≈40 ≙ beyond).

H1 (gradient-anchor staleness budget): SUPPORTED (budget ≈ 0) The dense gradient direction is essentially DECORRELATED even at the shortest lag (cos(g_t,g_{t−1})=0.018, cos(k≈5)=0.011, cos(k≈20)=0.004; sign-agreement 0.503→0.501 ≈ chance 0.5). The gradient-anchor staleness budget is effectively ZERO — a stale dense gradient is unusable at ANY latency on this task, well inside even the stable 5/5 cadence. The knee is at or below k=1.

H2 (drift is GRPO-coupled, not a pure parameter-point gap): SUPPORTED 9/10 rollout/logprob/response signals reach half their total drift at a lag ≤ the weight half-drift lag (≈7.9 global steps) — they drift on a comparable-or-FASTER timescale than the smooth parameter-point gap. Fastest: mean (t½≈1.0), max (t½≈1.0), pg_clipfrac (t½≈1.0) steps. The dangerous term is the distribution gap (gap 2), not just curvature×‖Δθ‖.

H3 (activation-codec staleness budget): SUPPORTED (staleness-insensitive) Boundary activation h: raw rank-90% ≈ 1.0 (top-1 singular dim holds 0.986 of the energy — a massive-activation outlier), mean-centered (residual) rank-90% ≈ 1.0 (vs r=77, H=1536). The signal is FAR below r — a rank-r activation codec is the right primitive and r is heavily OVER-provisioned. Top-77 overlap is essentially FLAT across lag (o(t,t−1)≈0.711 → o(t,t−20)≈0.706, ratio 0.99): the mismatch is PER-STEP, not staleness-driven, so codec STALENESS is not the limiter (Q is stale-tolerant); the constant ~0.71 offset is the noise-padded tail (h is ~rank-1, so the top-77 subspace is mostly noise beyond the energetic directions).

1What was run

A single short dense GRPO trajectory on the locked accel surface (comm-eff disabled — the dense control that was stable+monotonic to 100 steps in EXP-37D, val@100=0.7832). Two default-OFF measurement-only probes were enabled: a weight/gradient/optimizer-vector drift probe (FSDP full-param summon of selected decoder matrices) and a capture-only boundary-activation probe (forward+backward hooks dumping the boundary hidden-state h and its gradient grad_h). Both are strict no-ops when disabled (verified byte-identical to the pre-patch dense path in a 2-step off-parity gate) and never touch the optimizer, gradients, or activations.

3Gradient effective rank over training (nature of learning)

Dense-gradient stable rank + median rank-for-90%-energy over training, vs r=77 (no Big-Math epoch-2 split).

Median dense-gradient rank-for-90%-energy ≈ 78.0 (vs the locked PowerSGD rank r=77); median stable rank ‖g‖_F²/‖g‖₂² ≈ 3.2, participation ratio ≈ 8.8. Big-Math does not cross an epoch boundary in this 75-step run (train cap 20000 gives about 156 steps per epoch), so no epoch-2 split is reported. The dense gradient is effectively low-rank (≤ r), so a rank-r codec captures most of its energy.

Raw rank reflects the tensor the codec actually compresses; the top-1 energy share flags massive-activation outlier dimensions; the centered (residual) rank is the intrinsic signal rank a rank-r codec must track once the outlier/bias direction is removed.

This is the codec-decisive evidence the gradient-cosine curve cannot give: even if the gradient anchor is doomed as an optimizer signal, a rank-r activation codec with a slowly-rotating Q may still be the right compression primitive.

6GRPO-signal drift + correlation (H2: distribution-gap vs parameter-point gap)

Normalized lag-drift of behaviour/rollout signals vs the smooth weight drift. A curve that rises ABOVE the weight curve at small lag front-loads its drift = drifts faster.

Dense GRPO trajectory — reward and response-length over training (no epoch-2 boundary for this dataset).

H2 SUPPORTED 9/10 rollout/logprob/response signals reach half their total drift at a lag ≤ the weight half-drift lag (≈7.9 global steps) — they drift on a comparable-or-FASTER timescale than the smooth parameter-point gap. Fastest: mean (t½≈1.0), max (t½≈1.0), pg_clipfrac (t½≈1.0) steps. The dangerous term is the distribution gap (gap 2), not just curvature×‖Δθ‖.

The H2 test normalizes each signal's lag-k drift D(k)=median|x_t−x_{t−k}| to its own max-lag value and compares the half-drift lag (where the normalized curve reaches 0.5) against the weight half-drift lag (≈ 7.9 global steps). Behaviour signals that reach half their drift sooner than the (cumulative, smooth) weight drift are the signature of a distribution-gap (gap 2) danger rather than a pure curvature×‖Δθ‖ effect.

8Deliverable questions, answered

1. How fast do dense GRPO weights & gradients drift?

Weights drift smoothly/monotonically (§2 table). Gradient direction is already decorrelated at the shortest measured lag: cos 0.018 (k=1) → 0.011 (k≈5) → 0.004 (k≈20) → 0.001 (k≈40).

2. At what staleness does gradient cosine / sign agreement become unsafe?

The knee is at or BELOW k=1: the gradient is decorrelated immediately, so even the stable 5/5 anchor (k≈5) operates on a ~0-correlation gradient — the usable staleness budget is effectively zero on this task. This is consistent with the 20/20 failure AND implies even the 5/5 cadence is marginal here (cos(k≈5)=0.011).

3. Are the dangerous changes in gradient space, rollout/logprob space, response behaviour, or the boundary-activation subspace?

Gradient space carries a real, fast-decaying staleness term (H1). The boundary-activation forward subspace is staleness-INSENSITIVE (top-r overlap flat across lag), so codec staleness is NOT the danger there. Behaviour/rollout signals drift comparably-or-faster than the weights (H2 supported), so the dangerous term is the distribution gap (rollout/logprob/response space), not the parameter-point gap.

4. What does this imply for the next comm-eff PP method (compress in activation space, gradient space, or both)?

Activation space + the low-rank dense gradient. See §9.

5. Should future methods use the anchor only for Q/codec calibration, not as an optimizer gradient?

Yes. The stale gradient is a valid estimate for a policy that no longer exists; use the slow node as a Q/subspace calibrator instead.

6. What next-method families are plausible?

See §9 — frozen/slow-Q activation codec, cross-rank 2nd-moment objectives, curvature/2nd-order anchor use.

(v2-A) Is the boundary activation low-rank, and how fast does its top-r subspace rotate?

rank-90% ≈ 1.0 (vs r=77, H=1536) — far below r (≈rank-1; r over-provisioned); top-1 overlap o(t,t−20)=1.000, top-77 overlap o(t,t−20)=0.706 — flat across lag (staleness-insensitive) (§4); periodicity in §4. Backward grad_h rank-90% ≈ 180.0 (the forward/backward asymmetry).

(v2-B) Is the dense gradient low-rank, and how does its rank evolve?

rank-90% median ≈ 78.0; no epoch-2 split for this dataset (§3).

(v2-synthesis) Activation space, gradient space, or both — and should the anchor be a slow Q calibrator?

See §9.

9What to do next — recommendation

  • Do NOT use a stale dense gradient as an optimizer signal beyond a few ticks. The dense gradient direction de-correlates fast with lag (H1: cos 0.02→0.01→0.00 at k=1/5/20), so a delayed anchor is the gradient of a defunct policy — exactly the 20/20 failure. Use the anchor only as a slow Q / codec-calibration source (answers Q5: yes).
  • Compress the FORWARD boundary traffic in ACTIVATION space with a low-rank codec and a slowly-refreshed (or frozen) Q. The boundary activation is essentially rank-1 (a massive-activation direction dominates), so r=77 is heavily over-provisioned and its top-r subspace overlap is FLAT across lag (staleness-insensitive) — a frozen/periodically-refreshed PowerSGD-style Q tracks it cheaply; codec STALENESS is not the limiter.
  • Forward/backward asymmetry — do NOT assume the backward link is as compressible as the forward one. The forward activation h is ~rank-1, but the backward grad_h is rank-for-90% ≈ 180 > r=77: a rank-r codec on grad_h discards real energy. Budget the backward boundary codec at higher rank than the forward, or use error-feedback on the backward link.
  • Compress in activation space (low-rank forward boundary traffic) and exploit the low-rank dense gradient too; treat the slow node as a subspace/Q calibrator, not a gradient provider.
  • Because behaviour/rollout signals drift on a comparable-or-faster timescale than the weights (H2 supported), the staleness danger is the distribution gap, not the parameter-point gap — a codec/anchor that is correct in parameter space can still be stale in distribution space. The next method must be robust to rollout-distribution drift (e.g. on-policy Q refresh, or IS-style correction on any reused gradient signal).
  • Plausible next-method families for on-policy RLVR/GRPO: (a) frozen/slow-Q activation codec with on-policy refresh (forward link cheap, backward link higher-rank); (b) cross-rank 2nd-moment (disagreement-as-objective) routes that inject info outside the stale+current gradient means (the σ(M) ceiling); (c) curvature/2nd-order anchor use. Avoid reweighting/accumulating a stale gradient estimate (EXP-31/37 dead ends).

10Future-research signal inventory

This probe captured, and the next method's designer can mine WITHOUT a re-run:

  • Raw boundary h / grad_h (forward+backward boundary traffic) — any spectral/geometry analysis of the codec target.
  • g_dense per selected matrix — gradient spectrum / sign / cosine at finer lags.
  • update_vector (Δθ) + theta snapshots — effective vs nominal step, parameter-point gap.
  • Per-layer activation/grad L2 norms (all 28 decoder layers, sidecar_layernorms.jsonl) — where signal concentrates by depth.
  • GRPO scalars (reward, response length, pg_clipfrac, KL, advantage dispersion) from WandB — diversity-vs-rank, behaviour drift.
